description.narrative:
CARITAS Moroto under the ICSP will contribute to both impact 1 and 3 of the project. These are;
Impact 1: People experiencing poverty and most vulnerable to shocks, conflicts and crises have more sustainable and equitable access to food and livelihoods Impact 3:Institutional systems to prevent and respond to shocks, conflict and crises are more inclusive and better informed by the needs, rights and vulnerabilities of those furthest behind.
Specifically under impact are 1 Caritas Moroto will implement activities relatedto strengthening the sorghum value chain with an aim of improving food and income security for targeted groups and communities. These activities include training of small holder farmers good Sorghum agronomic practices, organizing of farmers in producer groups, creating awareness of land rights especially for women, and popularizing policies related to land, agriculture and climate change.
Under impact area 3 caritas will focus more on activities that contribute to timely response to disaster and shocks, localization ofresponse and activities aimed at Disaster Risk Reduction and preparedness. These include; Identification of community support structures essential for disaster risk mitigation, contingency planning and communitybased early warning, supporting integration of village level disaster management plans into parish, sub county and District disaster management plans, Facilitating Village and DistrictDisaster Management Committee meetings to monitor/review implementation of emergency mitigation and response plans and supporting surveillance to inform emergency response among others

participating-org.narrative:
HISTORY Caritas Moroto Diocese is the development arm of Moroto Diocese founded in 1981 as a relief agency to avert catastrophic drought and famine that hit Karamoja in 1979/1980. Subsequently, Caritas Moroto assumed a role of the main socio-economic development partner for the whole diocese.
In the recent years, Caritas Moroto has provided access to social, economic, cultural and political services for vulnerable communities in Karamoja. Its core programmes include humanitarian relief, agriculture, microfinance, water and sanitation, youth empowerment and peace building. The central feature of the projects is their community-based character to ensure local ownership and participation, as well as collaboration with Local Government for better sustainability. The Diocesan development arm has since transitioned interventions from emergency response to development work. However, the diocese still encounters someemergency needs e.g., relief food distribution during lean season and response to disease outbreaks like Ebola, cholera and COVID-19.
2. ACHIEVEMENTS Governments responsiveness to community needs has improved. This is caused by the routine monitoring of social services by Community Based Monitors (CBMS). The CBM approach implemented by CMDin partnership with CRS aims at promoting accountability in service delivery by government institutions (e.g., health facilities, community water points/boreholes, schools, sub counties and Districts) through routine monitoring of these facilities by volunteers based in communities to ensure the locals access social services. At the health facilities currently, there observed timely attendance to patients, timely delivery of drugs, proper storage and management, reduced absenteeism by health workers and health facility staffing has improved through advocacy to the government for increment of key staff at health facilities by the CBMs. CBMs also work with Water User Committees, School Management Committees and Health Unit Management Committees to ensure proper management of rehabilitated community water points, schools and health facilities to sustained quality service delivery to the communities.
Through the Male Change Agent (MCA) approach and community influencers, negative gender norms and harmful traditional practices like food taboos, early marriage and male dominance has been broken through sensitization, influencing and role modelling. Households reached with MCA interventions have embraced joint decision making,division of labour and shared roles and responsibilities. This has greatly contributed to prioritization of food security needs (decision to produce, sell and invest) at household level. Through sensitizations, training and demonstrations, farmers’ capacity has been built on natural resource management and disaster risk mitigation and response. Village disaster management committees that constitute community level disaster reporting and response structure for government were formed in 273 villages within the diocese to facilitate disaster reporting and response as per the requirement of the Uganda disaster management policy. Farmers’ capacity for agricultural production, post-harvest handling and management, marketing and linkage to input suppliers and off-takers has been built. Thishas greatly been done in the agricultural zone, however there still exist gaps in storage and marketing exhibited by weak governance and record keeping in the 5 existing bulking center. This is affecting crop commercialization. Farmers' access to credithas greatly improved through their involvement in group saving using Saving and Internal Lending Communities (SILC) methodology. At least 90% of the 54,000 participants/beneficiaries (adolescents, pregnant and lactating women and men) reached under Nuyok programme currently implemented by CMD in consortium with CRS and other partners are involved in group saving and borrowing and some groups have already been linked to financial institutions to access financial services.
Through Maternal Child HealthandNutrition (MCHN) trainings using the Mother Care Group (MCG) approach, household care givers have been trained on adoption of essential nutrition and hygiene actions to reduce prevalence of malnutrition at household level. Currently on average, 72% of mothers/ women reached with MCHN interventions in Napak, Nakapiripirit and Nabilatuk Districts consume diverse foods during pregnancy and lactation and 61% practice diarrhoea prevention strategies like observing the 5 critical moments of hand washing, presence of basic sanitary facilities like drying racks, latrines, practice appropriate water management, among others. 13 villages were declared open defecation free in early 2021 inNakapiripirit, Nabilatuk and Napak. this was achieved through sensitizationusing the Home Improvement Campaign (HIC) approach and these villages have since maintained open defecation status.
3. INSTITUTIONAL PURPOSE Vision: CMD envisions dignified, peaceful and self-reliant communities in Moroto Diocese.
Mission: To build the capacity of vulnerable households to ensure their sustainable livelihoods and human development guided by love, respect and commitment.
Core values: The core values of CMD are drawn from the social teaching of the Catholic Church as follows: a.Forgiveness and reconciliation by promoting “letting go” of the need to revenge and releasing negative thoughts of bitterness and resentment; restoration of friendly relations and key actions that make the views and beliefs compatible with one another. b. Transparency and accountability by operating in an accessible and open environment in dealing with all partners in a mutual way. It takes full responsibility for its actions and is answerable to all its stakeholders. c. Integrity by executing all itsactivities in an honest and truthful manner, and takes all reasonable measures to prevent wrongdoing by its management and staff. d. Respect for human rights by upholding the dignity of every person. e. Equality and equity by promoting gender participation, equity, stakeholder involvement and all-inclusive approaches in its development. f. Team work and institutional partnerships through upholding the spirit of working together and in partnership with other stakeholders. g. Mutual respect through appreciating the views held on issues of importance by every individual and partners.
Principle objectives: Strategic Focus Areas, Goals and Objectives for engagement for CMD are:
1. Livelihoods The goal of this focus area is to improve andsustain household food security and incomes through commercialized crop and livestock farming. The strategic objectives are: • enhanced commercialization of crop production, • enhanced commercialization of livestock, poultry, apiary production and productivity • enhanced trade orbusiness enterprises and entrepreneurship development and value chains.
2. Human Health and Nutrition The goal of this focus area is to have improved health of communities through good nutrition and reduced prevalence of preventable diseases. The strategic objective is improved and sustained nutrition status of pregnant and lactating women (PLW), adolescents’ girls and children under-five years in Karamoja.
3. Education The goal of this focus area is to have increased literacy levels and employable skills of school going children, youth and adults. The strategic objectives are: • Increased enrolment and retention of school going age pupils, • Skillsprovided to out-of-school youth and adults in Napak, Nabilatuk, Moroto, Amudat,and Nakapiripirit.
4. Water, Sanitation and Hygiene The goal of this focus area is to improve access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services for vulnerable communities. The strategic objectives are: • clean and safe drinking water provided tocommunities. • water for production provided to communities. •improved hygiene and sanitation at household, community and institution levels.
5. Land and Environmental Protection The goal of this focus area is to enhance community resilience and environment management. The strategic objectives are: • strengthened communityresilience to reduce vulnerability to climate shocks and stresses. • improved and sustained environmental management practices • enhanced stakeholder involvement in decision makingprocesses. • enhanced capacity of the land management institutions to ensure land justice is attained. • partner with cultural institutions to practically work for land justice within the local settings.
6. Social Protection The goal of this focus area is to enhance child protection and reduce gender-based violence. The strategic objectives are: • comprehensive case management services provided to gender-based violence survivors and increase communities’ knowledge on referral pathway. • enhanced capacity of women to participate in joint decision making at household and community levels. • strengthened gender, age and disability inclusion across respective programmes and service delivery. • reduced excessive alcohol and drug consumption at community and household level. • ensure security of persons and property.
7. Culture and Traditional Antiquities The goal ofthis focus area is to preserve the Karimojong cultural heritage for generational learning and guide future development interventions.The strategic objectives are: • Karimojong heritage and artefacts documented and preserved by 2025.Cultural literature of Karimojong documented • antiquity sites, art and cultural properties gazetted and preserved • Karimojong customary land and natural resources, e.g., ancestral burial grounds, elders shrines, grazing and hunting lands, mountains, stones, caves, natural trees (incense trees) preserved and protected • Improved Karimojong cultural industries – black smith, leather tanning, belts, gum Arabic – office glue processing. • Improved knowledge on traditional foods and ethno-medicines.
8. Cross-Cutting Areas The following cross-cutting areas whose strategic objectives and activities spread through two or more standalone but interrelated focus areas mentioned above have been incorporated where they fit best in the strategic focus areas: • Justice and Peace • Gender, Governance and Advocacy • Modern Technology • Institutional Development for Sustainability, and Infrastructural Development
Field(s) of activity: What are the principal thematic and geographic areas in which the organisation works? Who are the social actors that benefit from the work? CMD is thedevelopment arm of Moroto Diocese and its operations are limited to the geographical jurisdiction of the Diocese (Moroto, Napak, Nabilatuk, Nakapiripirit and Amudat Districts) and there may be no room for expansion to other Districts. While CMD has been operatingwith sub-offices established in the said Districts, the interventionsdonot cover all the villages because some are hard to reach. Hard to reach villages constitute roughly 15% of the total villages in which CMD could potentially implement crop production, livestock and apiary, health and nutrition, environmental protection,and social protection interventions. CMD will focus additional attention on the underserved villages like Chepkararat, Dungelech, Nabata, Namorupus, Aoyareng, Kawar, Alemutaba and Lokoma in Nakapiripirit District; Sakale, Kanangakinoi, Nakayot, Namonaloris andMoruangamion in Nabilatuk District, Apeitolim, Nyarkidi, Kokulonyo, Longaro, Komuturunyo, Iriiri, , Namoni, etc. in Napak District; Nanyidik, Lopelpel, Loyaraboth, Kakingol, Nakiloro, Nataparakwangan, Morukakori, Narengenya etc. in Moroto District; Loporokocho, Achorichor, Katabok etc. in Amudat District for inclusiveness and equity. Crop production, livestock and apiary, health and nutrition, environmental protection, and social protection activities.
Thematic areas of our work: Describe what you do ineach (as relevant) • Water Sanitation and Hygiene: CMD’s strategic objectives are to: a) Provide increased access to clean and safe drinking water to communities; b) Provide water for production; and c) Improve hygiene and sanitationat household, community and institutional levels.
Improved hygiene and sanitation behaviours and access to adequate safe and clean water by vulnerable communities. Due to inadequate knowledge and application of improved sanitation and hygienic practicesathousehold level and conflict that has displaced people across the region, access to water, sanitation and hygiene has remained a dauting challenge in Karamoja. The lack of access to clean and safe water and latrines leads to ingestion of pathogensthrough the “faecal-oral” route which then leads to diarrhoea, intestinal worms and environmental enteropathy. All of these infections result poorabsorption of nutrients by the body and poor health/nutrition outcomes. In Karamoja, stunting in children stands at 25.3%, whichis higher than the national average,15%. Poor nutrition indicators in the region are highly correlated with the low WaSH indicators with only 20% of the population able to access clean water. The districts of Napak, Moroto, Nabilatuk, Nakapiripirit score below 40% in sanitation and hygiene which is far below the national target of 77%. Only 27% of populations in Karamoja either wash their handsbefore food preparation or after visiting a latrine and approximately 73% do not have access to hand washingfacilities. However despite of the low sanitation and hygiene scores compared to the national average, sanitation and hygiene coverage has been improving e.g. Nabilatuk District increased from 9.8% in 2018 to 17% with safe watercoverage of58% in 2022,Nakapiripirit increased 22% in 2018 to 49% with safe water coverage of 58%, Napak District increased from 19% in 2018 to 37.5% with water coverage of 74% in 2022;these are the outcomes from hygiene and sanitation interventions such asNuyokand Integrated WaSH implemented by CMD, in addition toother interventions from local government. Over the years, CMD has supported community assets and structures such as functional hygiene and sanitation clusters, active water user committees, trainedhand pumpmechanics, good track record and work relationship withthe District local governments. CMD has taken advantage of them and made a solid contribution towards consolidation of the above hygiene and sanitation, and safe water coverage percentagesthat so far havebeen achieved but also expand to the neighbouring villages. CMD has three vastly experienced civil engineers currently managing WaSH interventions in Napak, Nakapiripirit and Amudat districts. CMD also has fully furnished sub-offices inthe said areasin addition to the equipment that are critical for project implementation.
• Livelihoods: The strategic objective is to enhance production, productivity and commercialization of crop, livestock, poultry and apiary valuechains in order to ensure increased household food and income. Through situation analysis and critical considerations, CMD has focused on the following areas as in sections Enhancing crop production, productivity and commercialization. Karamoja crop farming is mainlyrain-fed andthemaincrops grown are maize and Sorghum. Other crops grown include sunflower, beans, sweet potatoes, ground nuts, cassava, among others. Crop farming is subsistence in nature, though there’s increasing market orientation in recent years;especially along thegreen belt (agricultural zone) on the western part of Karamoja. In contrast to the mixed livestock/agriculture livelihoods of the past, crop farming is increasingly the primary form of livelihood especially in Napak, Nabilatukand Nakapiripirit Districtsas sedentary settlement increases, and crop farming and drying/post-harvest practices improve. This is associated with the farmer capacity building interventions by CMD and the District local governments. CMD in its agricultural interventions built the capacity of Producer Marketing Groups in the agricultural and agro-pastoral zones in basic agronomy, post-harvest handling, linkage to agro-input suppliers and off-takers through the Private Agricultural Service Providers (PASPs) trained under Nuyok programmeto provide agricultural extension services to farmers at a fee, established a functional sunflower and honey processing plant in Lorengechora under IFSP project funded by CAFOD to support value addition, linked farmers to tractorhire services to increasecrop acreage etc.
CMD seek to consolidate the above achievements through; strengthening bulking, storage and linkage to off-takers, scale up value addition (processing and packaging) of essential marketable agricultural products and marketing, in addition to strengthening agricultural extension support to farmers and investments in climate-smart options especially in hard-to-reach areas. CMD continues to build the capacity of farmers in hard-to-reach areas forincreasedcrop production and productivity through promotion of high value crops and increasing market orientation for improved household income.
Farmers’ capacity building on honey processing and marking (Honey and Honey products). Karimojong incomesources continue to widen / broaden as population numbers rise and poverty increases. For example, poor households and individuals are resorting to offering casual labour, firewood selling and charcoal burning, vegetablegrowing for sale, artisanal mining and stonequarrying to earn a living. This has negative consequences on the environment. In addition to livestock keeping and crop especially cereal production, Karamojong communities (especially Tepeth communities in Moroto and Bokora in Napak, Pokot in Amudat and Kadamaof Nakapiripirit) produce alot of honey that is mostly sold to local middlemen unprocessed who later make big margins after processing and packaging. CMD with funding from CAFOD established a honey processing unit in Lorengechora toenable farmers to process and package their honey and sell at higher prices; this processing unit is only in Napak District.
Capacity building of farmers and CAHWs on improved animal rearing practices and CAHW business model. Karamoja has had a long history of cross-border livestock diseaseoutbreaks (e.g. Foot and Mouth Disease, Pestes depetits Ruminantes, Contagious Bovine Pleuro Pneumonia etc.) and when such outbreaks occur, attempts by the government through the mainstream extension and CommunityAnimal Health Workers(CAHWs) to control escalationare unsatisfactory and unsuccessful due to inadequate and poor quality of extension services inadequate drugs supplies, sometimes poor diagnosis, and high Farmer to extension worker ratio. In the pastten years, a number ofCAHWs were trained, equipped with start-up kits containing assorted drugs and veterinary equipment. CMD focuses on building farmers capacity to improve animal rearing practices, farmers sensitization on the fee for services model for veterinaryservices and providingrefresher training to CAHWs on livestock health, disease reporting, control and CAHW model as a business for continuity. We make use of the Veterinary doctor and animal husbandry professionals and the community-based livestock agents that CMD has empowered, to deliverthe planned livestock interventions.
• Health:
Under this theme, CMD envisions sustainable improvement in health and nutrition status of pregnant and lactating mothers, adolescent girls and children under fiveyears.
Enhancing uptake of sexual and reproductive Health services, increased adoption of MIYCAN practices and capacity building of VHTs and health units to strengthen community linkage and referral. Karamoja population is young with the average age being 15 years; half of the 1.2 million inhabitants being females with the highest total fertility rate; women aged 15-49 years giving birth to an average of 8 children, higher than Uganda’s average of 5. While access to universal health care is importantfor human capital developmentand wellbeing,the health sector in Karamoja region is still lagging behind due to limited access to health services, sparsely distributed populations especially resettlement areas of CMD operating areas, fewerhealth facilities and consistently poor performance inkey health indicators due to low capacityof health teams and HUMCs to manage health facilities , inadequate drug supplies and inadequate health staff . Teenage pregnancy continues to greatly affect education, social and economic wellbeing ofyoungpeople. Early parenting reduces the likelihood of female adolescents to complete high school and pursue the necessary post-secondary education. One in every four adolescent girls in Karamoja has had their first child; putting the teenage pregnancy rate at 24 percentand the major drivers are; limited access and low uptake of reproductive health services, poverty, early, forced and child marriage. Karamoja’s food and nutrition security situation has beendeteriorating since 2020 with the population in IPCAFI Phase 3 or above increasing from 27% in June 2020, to 30% in April 2021 and to 41% in April 2022 with 9,500 pregnant women projected to be acutely malnourished for the period February 2022-January 2023. Outof the total children screened for malnutrition ((249,859) in the first round, 3.2 percent (9,306) and 13.9 percent (40,919) of thechildren screened were severely and moderately malnourished respectively and these households employ crisis and emergency coping strategies during lean periods.The above gaps havebeen addressed by; 1) Enhancing uptake of Adolescent, sexual and reproductive Healthservices (ASRHS) by pregnant, lactating women and adolescents; 2) Capacity building of VHTs and Health unit management committees to strengthen health facility andcommunity linkages and referral, and 3) Capacity building of households to increase adoption of Maternal, Infant, Young child and Adolescent Nutrition (MIYCAN) practices. The identification of the three outcomeareas is guided by theurgent need tocontribute to the national health indicators and SDGs by 2030; especially SDG 3 (Ensuring healthy lives and promotingwellbeing for all). CMD is a faith-based organisation with a strong collaborationand partnership with local stakeholders, has adequate physicalassets necessary for successful project implementation, competent health and nutrition professionals, capacity and experience to implement diverse programmes, strong internal control systems and has potentialto build synergies with Caritasnetworks.
•Protection, Peace building, Social Cohesion: Despite the governments’ and Non-governmental organisations efforts to enhance resilience in Karamoja through economic empowerment, resilienceto climate change, education and skills, communities havefailed to be fully incorporated in the development projects due to low education as manifested by low enrolment of both boys and girls in schools and low retention of girls in school, heavy women's workload, Neglected Young People with nothing todo, Gender-Based Violence(GBV), earlygirl child marriages, Female Genital Mutilation, Child Labour and HIV/AIDS discrimination. However, to enhance safeguarding and reduce gender-based violence there isneed to strengthenmind-set change through trainings for men, youth, traditional leaders and women to change men’s perception towards women participation in community and development activities. There’s also need to work with women, girls, men and boys in the promotion ofgender equalityand empowerment, promotion of positive masculinities as well as empowering girls and women, and ensuring that there is a focus on social norms change and the needed steps towards wider social change. CMD willcontinue to invest heavily onbuilding resilience to strengthen the move away from “hand-outs” towards enhancing capacities to takeadvantage of opportunities to engage in productive work and employment for women and youths.
• Environment and Energy: While CMDhas the relevant experience and expertise through its staff currently implementing the resilience component under Nuyok Programme, there are functional village level disaster management committees in areas covered by Nuyok.
Capacity building of local governments and community structures on Sustainable LandManagement (SLA). One in every three people on earth is in some way affected by land degradation. Latest estimates indicate that nearly 2 billion hectares of land worldwide are already seriously degraded. This includes large areas of crop land, grassland, woodland and forest areas whose degradation reduces productivity, disrupts vital ecosystem functions, negatively affects biodiversity and water resources, and increases vulnerability to climate change. As a country,Uganda has seenan increase in deforestation in the last decade. While in 2001, the country lost 297km2 of forest, by 2020 the figure had more thandoubled to 736km2 of forest lost a year. In the last 25 years, Uganda has lost 63 percent of its forest cover due to tree-cutting for firewood,timber andcharcoal,as well as the growth of farms and towns and approximately 41 percent of Uganda’s total land area isexperiencing degradation, with soil erosion being the most common form of degradation , with Karamoja on the receiving end of many of these negative effects because of its vulnerability to the effects of climate change compared to other regions, leading to widespread and protracted food and nutrition insecurity, and hunger. Thousands of people inKaramoja sub-region are at risk of losing theirlivelihoods due to the rapid degradation of pastoral rangeland in the region and the causes of degradation being; poor land use andmanagement practices i.e., monoculture, soil erosion due to floods, sheet erosion, animal hoofs trampling, cutting of treesfor construction ofmanyattas, charcoal burning, bush burning, firewood among others. There have, however, been several attempts by the government (both central and local) and non-Government actors to ensure local communities are sensitised on the dangers of environmentaldestruction and the associated natural disasters, but this has not yielded much results because; there is lack of capacity by the local Governments to promote sensitizations and enforce sustainable land use management, inadequacies of structures at lower/village levels to coordinate disaster reporting, the existing information gap most especially on the existing policy frameworks and weak enforcement of the existing environmental protection policy frameworks. Sustainable Land Management (SLM) is crucial to minimising land degradation, rehabilitating degraded areas and ensuring the optimal use of land resources for the benefit of present and future generations. CMD bases its sustainable land managementapproach on four common principles; Land-user-driver and participatory approaches, Integrated use of natural resources at ecosystem and farming system levels, multi-stakeholder involvement, and policy and institutional support.
• Education: The objectives under this strategic areaof focus are to; a) Increase enrolment and retention of school going age pupils; b) Skill out-of-school youth and adults. At the moment CMD has no active projects on education.
• Others – specify Culture and TraditionalAntiquities Given the current scramble formineral concessions in Karamoja by multinational corporations and the fact that there is rapid influence from other migrants and tribes into Karamoja, there is real dangerand a high risk of destroying antiquitysites, displacement of local people from their customary lands and destruction of local cultural values by assimilation. Caritas Moroto Diocese has in a pipeline a project that seeks to contribute to; a) Documentation and preservation of Karimojongheritage, artefacts and literature; b)Promotion ofgazetting and preservation of the antiquity sites, art, cultural values and cultural industries; c) Promote industry, preservation and protection of Karimojong customary land, natural resources, traditional foods,ethno-medicines,music, dance and drama, film, etc.
Cross-cutting areas: Six cross-cutting areas are embedded within the stand-alone areas of focus and these include; Justice and Peace, Gender and safeguarding, Governance and Advocacy, Technologyand Innovation, Institutional Development for Sustainability and Infrastructural Development.
Areas of operation: Refer to “Field(s) of activity” 4.STRATEGIC POSITIONING Analyse the environment in which the organisation works? Who are the other relevant social actors, including government and business, andwhat roles do they play? In this context, what is unique about the position of the organisation? The partners operating in “our” area are Save the Children, UNICEF, World Vision, ZOA, Irish Aid,WFP, TMF, ISP, C<(>&<)>D, Enabel and Straight Talk Foundation. The uniqueness’s of CMD are the field offices operating in hard-to-reach areas with staff hired on the ground operating in the villages and fleet available and based in those areas; at the main office in Moroto sits the operation department.
CMD has a fleet of vehicles, motorbikes, office equipment, offices in all the five districts of the diocese; closer to the disadvantaged communities, rich experience implementing agricultural interventions and the required technical expertise in a pool of its human resources, has good visibility at community level, strong financial control systems, good organisational reputation and collaboration with other stakeholders.
5. FUNCTIONALORGANISATIONAL CHART include below your organisational chart) How are authority and responsibilities structured? For each operational unit, indicate the job titles, number of people in each position, and if they are men or women. CMD organisational structure was recently reconfigured and alignedto 2021-2025strategic plan. It is composed of the Bishop, the commission, Caritas Director, Head of Programmes (not present at the moment but CMD hired Coordinators and Lead PMs), HR manager, and Finance and Administration Manager (FAM) The Bishop’s responsibility is to coordinate all fivediocesan departments / desks namely Caritas, education, health, justice and peace, land desk. He oversees all the diocesan activities in all the elevenparishes ofthe Diocese. The Bishop has to be informed about all personnel matters, any events that areout of routine and is briefed about any matter regarding the department that he wishes to look into.
The Caritas Commission is responsible to the Bishop and it’s a body composed of seven members appointed by the Bishop to makepolicies and oversee their implementation, play advisory role to management and the Bishop, recruit staff, approve and ensure that CMD policies are in line with the Diocesan development Plan, support the Director in lobbying and fundraising and review and approve annual and quarterly plans, budgets and reports. The Caritas Commission has 03 committees (Procurement, Human resource and Finance) undertaking related but complementary roles.
The Caritas Director reportsto the Commission Chairperson. He /she oversees the overall management and performance of the Caritas Moroto Diocese and to ensure Caritas development direction is in line with the mission of the Diocese through;planning, coordinatingand controlling program activities, identifying and working out appropriate development projects for CMD in collaboration with the program management team (PMT) and identifies contacts, collaborates with donors and other funding agencies for the good of the organisation. The CMD Director supervisesthe operations and the Head of Programmes who oversees all Programmes, initiates and reviews programs and ensures project /Programobjectives are achieved in collaboration with the Programme Management team (Director, HOP, FAM, HRM/O, PLM/O, Programme/Project Managers).
The Programs management team is directly responsible for programming and implementation of Program /project activities. The team is led by the Head of Programmes witha direct reporting lineto the Executive Director. Project Managers and the MEAL Manager report directly to the Head of Programmes. Officers (MEAL, Agronomy, Gender, Community planning, Livestock, SILC, DRR, NRM, Health systems strengthening, Nutrition, WaSH, ICT4D all report to the respective Managers in the line Department/Purposes. The field supervisors and assistants who are responsible for field agents report to the officers in the Departments they are attached to.
The operations team headed by the HR Manager and FAM oversee and support service delivery and the flowof resources and information within theorganisation. additionally, the operations team is responsible for the following; Procurement and Logistics officer, projects accountant, Finance and Administration assistants/officers, procurement and logistics assistants, drivers, office assistants and securityguards. This structure has clearly outlined lines of authority, reporting and roles and responsibilities for each position aimed ateffectiveness in communication and program delivery and results.
